question: Amani has 3 life. Briar casts [Chain of Plasma], targeting Amani. As it resolves, Amani pays the cost to copy it, and chooses to have the copy target Campbell. What happens?
answer:
Direct answer: Chain of Plasma deals 3 damage to Amani, dropping Amani to 0 life. Amani doesn't die immediately, because state-based actions (like a player losing for 0 or less life) aren't checked in the middle of a spell's resolution — no player gets priority while Chain of Plasma is resolving [608.2g]. So Amani still gets the chance to discard a card and copy Chain of Plasma, and that copy is put on the stack targeting Campbell, with Amani as its controller and owner [707.10d]. Once Chain of Plasma finishes resolving and a player would receive priority, Amani loses the game for having 0 life.

Details:
- The copy is a spell even though there's no card for it, and it copies all of Chain of Plasma's characteristics and choices, except that Chain of Plasma's own text lets the discarding player choose a new target — here Campbell [707.10d]. Amani must actually have a card in hand to discard; if not, no copy is made (the discard and copy are both "may," per Chain of Plasma's text).
- The copy is controlled by Amani, not Briar [707.10d]. Note that Chain of Plasma's own wording (the player dealt damage may discard and copy) is what puts a copy under an opponent's control; that card text governs.
- When the copy resolves, it deals 3 damage to Campbell, and then Campbell may discard a card to copy it again and choose a new target — the "chain" continues.
- Timing note: I'm assuming Amani was at 3 life when the damage was dealt, so the damage is lethal but only takes effect after resolution. If Amani had been at 4+ life, nothing about the copy changes; Amani simply survives at 1.

One gap: the provided rules don't cover what happens to objects controlled by a player who leaves the game, so I can't tell you from this context whether Amani's copy on the stack is removed when Amani loses. The copy will already be on the stack targeting Campbell before Amani's loss is checked [707.10d]; look up the "leaves the game" rules for the aftermath.

Multiplayer: this scenario already involves at least three players (Briar, Amani, Campbell), and Chain of Plasma's redirection works the same way regardless of table size; with only two players the copy could only be aimed back at Briar, Briar's permanents, or Amani's own permanents.

Then the player who would have received priority does so.

answer_gold: The copy is put onto the stack targeting Campbell. Then the original Chain of Plasma finishes resolving and state-based actions are checked. Amani loses the game, and the copy of Chain of Plasma is removed from the stack before it would resolve.

question: Alex controls a [Phantasmal Image] that's a copy of [Elvish Warrior]. There are no creatures other than Phantasmal Image on the battlefield. Alex casts [Wispweaver Angel]. Do they have to sacrifice Phantasmal Image?
answer:
Yes — Alex must target Phantasmal Image, and it will be sacrificed.

Why: Wispweaver Angel's ability, "When this creature enters, you may exile another target creature you control, then return that card to the battlefield under its owner's control," is a triggered ability with a target. Targets are declared as the ability is put on the stack, not on resolution [115.1], and a triggered ability's controller puts it on the stack the next time a player would receive priority [603.3c]. The word "may" governs whether the exile-and-return happens when the ability resolves; it does not make choosing a target optional. Since Phantasmal Image (currently a copy of Elvish Warrior) is the only "another creature you control" available, it is the only legal target and must be chosen.

Phantasmal Image's copy effect gives it "When this creature becomes the target of a spell or ability, sacrifice it" in addition to Elvish Warrior's copied characteristics. Targeting it with Wispweaver Angel's trigger causes that sacrifice ability to trigger; it goes on the stack above Wispweaver Angel's trigger and resolves first, and Alex sacrifices Phantasmal Image.

Then Wispweaver Angel's trigger tries to resolve. Its only target is no longer on the battlefield, so that target is illegal and the ability doesn't resolve at all [608.2b]. Nothing is exiled or returned. (Even if Alex could somehow decline, the "may" choice would be made only on resolution [608.2d], far too late to save Phantasmal Image.)

If instead there had been no other creature you control at all, Wispweaver Angel's trigger would simply have no legal target and would be removed from the stack.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count: it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since the ability only targets a creature Alex controls.

question: Ashley controls [Skill Borrower] and [Sensei's Divining Top]. The top card of their library is a [Putrid Leech]. Ashley activates Skill Borrower's ability, then activates Sensei's Divining Top's first ability, choosing to put Putrid Leech second from the top. Then they activate Sensei's Divining Top again, putting Putrid Leech back on top. Can Ashley activate Skill Borrower's ability again?
answer:
No. Ashley can't activate that ability a second time this turn.

Skill Borrower gains Putrid Leech's ability "Pay 2 life: This creature gets +2/+2 until end of turn. Activate only once each turn" while Putrid Leech is the revealed top card (Skill Borrower's own text tells you to play with the top card of your library revealed and grants all activated abilities of that card, with name references treated as Skill Borrower's name — see rule 201.5b). The "Activate only once each turn" restriction is part of the ability as gained, and by rule 602.5b/602.5c that restriction applies to the object that has the ability — here Skill Borrower — and a player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated (602.5). Ashley already activated it once this turn with Skill Borrower, so the prohibition still applies.

Shuffling Putrid Leech down and back up with Sensei's Divining Top doesn't help. Even though the card technically becomes a new object when it stops being revealed and is revealed again (401.6), the once-per-turn restriction is tracked on Skill Borrower, the permanent whose ability was activated, not on the library card. Nothing resets that count. (Compare rule 700.10, which likewise tracks activation by the permanent that was the source.)

Timing note: I'm assuming the first Skill Borrower activation (the Putrid Leech pump) fully happened before the Sensei's Divining Top activations. If instead Ashley had never activated the gained pump ability this turn, they could activate it now while Putrid Leech is back on top. Also note that under Skill Borrower ruling #4, if the top card changes while you're in the middle of activating a gained ability, the ability still resolves — but that doesn't grant an extra use.

This answer doesn't depend on player count; it works the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

question: Avery controls [Corpsejack Menace] and casts [Rescuer Sphinx], choosing to return Corpsejack Menace to their hand. How many +1/+1 counters will Rescuer Sphinx enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Rescuer Sphinx enters with just one +1/+1 counter.

Why: Rescuer Sphinx's "As this creature enters, you may return a nonland permanent you control to its owner's hand. If you do, this creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it" is a replacement effect that modifies how Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield ([614.1c]), and the choice of whether and what to return is made before Rescuer Sphinx is actually on the battlefield ([614.12a], [Rescuer Sphinx ruling #2]). Applying that effect actually moves Corpsejack Menace to its owner's hand ([614.13a] — an effect modifying how a permanent enters may cause other objects to change zones).

Corpsejack Menace's ability ("If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature you control, twice that many +1/+1 counters are put on it instead") is also a replacement effect, and replacement effects are not locked in ahead of time — they apply continuously as events happen ([614.1d], [615.1]). By the time the event "Rescuer Sphinx enters with a +1/+1 counter on it" occurs, Corpsejack Menace is already in Avery's hand, so its doubling ability no longer exists on the battlefield to apply. Only effects that already exist and would apply are considered ([614.12]). So no doubling: one counter, put on Rescuer Sphinx by Avery as its controller ([122.6a]).

Sequencing note: the return and the counter come from the same single replacement effect, so no player can act in between ([Rescuer Sphinx ruling #2]) — Avery cannot keep Corpsejack Menace around "just long enough" to double. Had Avery instead returned some other nonland permanent and left Corpsejack Menace on the battlefield, Rescuer Sphinx would enter with two counters instead ([Corpsejack Menace ruling #0]), and with four if two Corpsejack Menaces were present ([Corpsejack Menace ruling #1]).

Player count doesn't matter here: all the choices belong to Avery alone, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game (APNAP order under [101.4] would only matter if multiple players had simultaneous choices).

answer_gold: Two. Both cards have a replacement effect. Avery will choose whether they are returning a permanent, but won't actually complete the action until Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield. Therefore Corpsejack Menace will still apply to the +1/+1 counter being from Rescuer Sphinx's ability.

question: Ainsley controls [Spellweaver Volute] that's enchanting [Cruel Truths] in their graveyard. What zone is Spellweaver Volute in?
answer:
Spellweaver Volute is on the battlefield. It's an Aura enchantment permanent, so it sits on the battlefield even though the object it enchants — Cruel Truths — is a card in a graveyard, a different zone [Spellweaver Volute ruling #2] [Spellweaver Volute ruling #4]. Spellweaver Volute is unusual in that its enchant ability ("Enchant instant card in a graveyard") attaches it to something that is neither a permanent nor a player; card text like this overrides the general expectation that an Aura is attached to something on the battlefield [303.4b].

So: Spellweaver Volute — battlefield; Cruel Truths — Ainsley's graveyard. Spellweaver Volute is not itself in the graveyard, and Cruel Truths is not on the battlefield [Spellweaver Volute ruling #2].

This only changes if Cruel Truths leaves the graveyard (cast, exiled, shuffled away, etc.). Then Spellweaver Volute is attached to an illegal/nonexistent object and is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action, which doesn't use the stack [704.5m] [704.1] [Spellweaver Volute ruling #5]. The same happens if Spellweaver Volute ends up attached to nothing [Spellweaver Volute ruling #0]. Note also that an Aura can't enchant a card outside its controller's range of influence in multiplayer games; with only two players that restriction never matters [801.8].

cited_text.303.4b: Some enchantments have the subtype “Aura.” An Aura enters the battlefield attached to an object or player. What an Aura can be attached to is defined by its enchant keyword ability (see rule 702.5, “Enchant”). Other effects can limit what a permanent can be enchanted by. The object or player an Aura is attached to is called enchanted. The Aura is attached to, or “enchants,” that object or player.
cited_text.704.5m: The state-based actions are as follows: If an Aura is attached to an illegal object or player, or is not attached to an object or player, that Aura is put into its owner’s graveyard.
cited_text.704.1: State-based actions are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions (listed below) are met. State-based actions don’t use the stack.
cited_text.801.8: An Aura can’t enchant an object or player outside its controller’s range of influence. If an Aura is attached to an illegal object or player, the Aura is put into its owner’s graveyard as a state-based action. See rule 704.

answer_gold: Spellweaver Volute is on the battlefield. The game doesn't require an Aura to be in the same zone as the object it's attached to.
